summary.text: A polymer is a material made of very large molecules built from many repeating subunits derived from monomers.
Polymers can be natural, like DNA and proteins, or synthetic, like the plastic polystyrene.
Their large molecular mass gives them unique physical properties including toughness and high elasticity.

items.prompt: A chemist links many small molecules into one huge molecule. What are the small building blocks called?
items.explain: Polymers are created by polymerization of many small molecules known as monomers.

items.prompt: Terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol join to make PET polyester, and the repeat unit matches the two monomers minus two water molecules. What does this show?

options.label: Monomers always join with nothing lost
Water is the repeating unit of the polyester
Some chemical groups can be lost from each monomer during polymerization
Only one of the two monomers ends up in the chain

items.explain: During polymerization some chemical groups may be lost from each monomer, as with PET.

items.prompt: In one method, whole chains of monomers combine directly with one another, as in making polyester. Which category of synthesis is this?
items.explain: In step-growth polymerization chains of monomers may combine directly, while in chain polymerization monomers are added one at a time.

items.prompt: A factory heats natural rubber with sulfur and gets vulcanized rubber. What does this show about commercial polymers?

options.label: They are all built from scratch from monomers
Many are made by chemically modifying natural polymers
They are never based on natural materials
They always need a catalyst to be modified

items.explain: Many commercially important polymers are made by chemical modification of natural ones, such as vulcanized rubber from natural rubber and sulfur.

items.prompt: A friend says all polymers are man-made plastics. Which example is the best counterexample?
items.explain: Polymers include natural biopolymers such as DNA and proteins as well as synthetic ones like polystyrene.

items.prompt: A material has a backbone built on silicon atoms instead of carbon. Which is an example?
items.explain: Elements such as silicon form silicones, examples being Silly Putty and waterproof plumbing sealant, while polyethylene has a carbon backbone and polyethylene glycol and DNA have oxygen in theirs.

steps.text: PET polyester is made from terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol.
Its repeating unit corresponds to the two monomers combined, with two water molecules lost.
So the repeat unit must contain every atom of both monomers.
The piece of each monomer that is incorporated is called the repeat unit.

paragraphs.heading: Many parts
paragraphs.text: A polymer is a material built from huge molecules, called macromolecules, each made of many repeating subunits. The subunits come from small molecules called monomers, which polymerization links into a chain or network held together by covalent bonds. The piece of each monomer that ends up inside the polymer is called a repeat unit, or monomer residue. The word itself comes from Greek words meaning many and part.

paragraphs.heading: Natural and synthetic
paragraphs.text: Polymers come in two types: those found in nature and those people make. Synthetic examples include plastics such as polystyrene, the stuff of styrofoam, while natural ones include the polyisoprene of latex rubber, the cellulose in wood and paper, and DNA and proteins. In living things, essentially all large biological molecules, namely proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides, are polymers or largely built from them. Their wide range of properties gives both kinds essential roles in everyday life.

paragraphs.heading: Why size matters
paragraphs.text: Polymer molecules are very heavy compared with small molecules, and this gives them unusual physical properties: toughness, high elasticity, viscoelasticity, and a habit of forming amorphous and semicrystalline structures instead of crystals. In plastics the continuously linked backbone is mostly carbon. Polyethylene is a simple case, with ethylene as its repeat unit. Other backbones exist: silicon forms silicones such as Silly Putty, and oxygen sits in the backbones of polyethylene glycol, polysaccharides and DNA.

paragraphs.heading: How polymers are made
paragraphs.text: During polymerization, some chemical groups can be lost from each monomer. PET polyester shows this: its monomers are terephthalic acid and ethylene glycol, and its repeating unit equals the two combined minus two water molecules. Synthetic methods fall into two families. In chain polymerization monomers join one at a time, as in polystyrene, while in step-growth polymerization chains of monomers can link directly to each other, as in polyester. Step-growth includes polycondensation, which forms a low-molar-mass by-product at every step, and polyaddition.

paragraphs.heading: An old material, a new idea
paragraphs.text: People used natural polymers for centuries, among them hemp, shellac, amber, wool, silk and natural rubber. Cotton, starch and rubber were familiar long before synthetic polymers like polyethene and perspex reached the market. Jöns Jacob Berzelius coined the word polymer in 1833, though his meaning differed from today's definition. In 1920 Hermann Staudinger proposed the modern idea of polymers as large covalently bonded molecules, and spent the next decade gathering experimental evidence for it.

paragraphs.heading: Polymers at industrial scale
paragraphs.text: Synthetic polymers, listed roughly by world demand, include polyethylene, polypropylene, polystyrene, polyvinyl chloride, synthetic rubber and nylon. In 2015 more than 330 million tons of them were made. Many commercially important polymers start from natural ones. Nitric acid turns cellulose into nitrocellulose, and heating natural rubber with sulfur gives vulcanized rubber.
